videos.transcript_text: - There are decades where nothing happens and weeks where decades happen. And we have seen decades of progress happen in the last nine months. And now, dear friends, here's DHH. 13 months ago, we sat down right here to talk about programming, and then everything changed. That doesn't exist for me as an emotional component. It is only there as an intellectual component, and the emotional component for me is 100% pure, unadulterated joy- ... and optimism and amazement that we've made computers do this. I mean, imagine you're there when the Wright brothers take flight. If you zoom out and look at all of human history, how many humans got to live within the same epoch that they were born in? They never saw that complete change of the world and of society. Yeah, the... And it really just sh- shifted for many great developers. Now, the chatbot I actually liked, as we talked about. Great tutor right from the get-go, great way of looking things up on the internet, not what was gonna replace me chiseling code. But- ... then we get the agents. And the agents start out being curiosities for about five minutes, and then they get amazing, and then they get, "Oh my God, is this AGI?" And all of that happened since last year, even just within the last nine months. We have basically these few phases here. We have AI in the pre-agentic era. I was still chiseling code, I just had a little helper, a little sidekick- ... who could bounce ideas off, and I could look up this information online and so forth in a more efficient way. It was just a more efficient way to do what I was already doing, and it didn't change the emotional connection I had to the computer. Then we get to November 24th, 2025. This agent harness question where I don't know if Opus 4.5 was that much smarter than Opus 4, which is what we had in the summer, but its ability to instrument your computer, to use tools, to check its own work, to apply its intelligence in such a way that you could get real meaningful work out of it, was completely different. And I think this is then the big change that happens for almost anyone who paid attention and started playing with it over the Christmas break. This is what I heard- ... from Shopify and other places with lots of employees who suddenly had a breather, suddenly had a couple of weeks to lean back and just look at what was going on, gave it a try, and had the same mind-blowing experience that these agents were of a different genre than what we had before. And then what we get to is, I'm already excited at this point. Like, by December, I'm already revisiting sort of all my priors- ... and going like, "Wow, if it can do this, can it also do that?" "Oh, yeah, it can." And again, Opus 4.5 now looks like a retarded model. And this is the magic of this progress, is you think you've reached something... I remember thinking at the moment, "If this is the last model we get, I'll be set. I'll be happy." Because it was not just about it being able to solve a task, it was also that I could look at its path there and go, "Yep. Yep. Maybe not there, but almost," and it would give you two notes. You'll get to where I wanted to go in the way I wanted to go there. You could produce code I wanted to merge. You could produce code that actually looked beautiful if it was written in Ruby. Rust, different question. But this ability for the agents to truly become an extension of how I wanted to work was very novel. But then we wait just until early spring, and suddenly we get sub-agents. We get harnesses that can subdivide the task, and something that would take Opus quite a while suddenly took a fifth of the time, a tenth of the time, because it could get chopped up and suddenly you got eight sub-agents working for you. But both of those two first phases of the agentic age, to me, still felt like I had to drive. I could tell it what I wanted, where to look for it, and steer it a little bit when it went off, and then we'll get there, and I would go much faster. But I had to be in the driver's seat. I'm telling it the problem I have. I'm telling it the fuzzy, vague idea I have. It tells me where we're going. It tells me which path to take, and I will still look at it because I'm a curious person and I like computers and I like the outcome of it, but I really kinda don't have to. In fact, the cars now just drive themselves, right? And this is where we've arrived at now, that I can trust. For the domain I'm working in right now, I can trust it, and feel completely confident that it's gonna have my back. Now, that's also a point where I've stressed many times that when people accuse vibe coders of being slob generators, I go right back at them and say, "Have you looked at the average programmer's output?" That is some other slob too. If you've looked at behind the scenes of many great companies and what their code bases look like after there's been 3,000 humans through them, they're awful. Absolutely awful. - Can you tell me the intuition you have? I seem to just, stepping back and observing the different apps that we all rely on, I don't know, Adobe Photoshop, all this kind of stuff. The implementation part is only a small segment of it. The other thing I'd say is that most organizations don't know what they want. They don't know how to make it better. And if you don't have those element in excess of your implementational capacity, it doesn't help. So you can make a lot of shitty ideas come true, then what? Are you gonna ship that? If you step back for a moment and think of the towering organizations we have who have had tens of thousands of programmers at their disposal. I mean, I'm picking on Microsoft here. It's just a clanker, and the clanker won't mind. In fact, the producers of clankers, the labs, love when you spend tokens in vain. They get paid just the same. Not only do we get this wealth of glorious pull requests made by agents with all the boxes ticked, we also get to tap into a creativity of people who did not have access to contribute to a project before. Otherwise, those ideas would just have lived inside their heads. Again, Is- that is not the purpose of open source, that we tap into the collective intelligence and creativity of the whole goddamn planet, and we channel that towards a commons where we all benefit from the combined efforts of everyone. I thought all the ideas would originate with the humans. They would tell their agents what to build, and off they went. I don't think that's true anymore at all. Of course, it's easy to get bogged down again in the flood of flashy demonstrations, benchmark results, and Claude-designed animations.  I fully admit that I am not immune to that either, as I spent hours exploring a Final Fantasy-like playable world, designed for me by Opus 5.5 in the Unreal engine, which I published.  The truth is that this may not be the most appropriate time to delve into these matters, as there is a lot of other news, relating to Opus and other things , that is worth considering. Each one of them, if I 'm being honest, probably deserves a two- hour documentary. This sometimes makes me honestly wonder whether it suits AI officials to have this flood of news, both good and bad, because it may be obscuring the fact that many labs made crucial promises that they are now, let's say, beginning to change.  Naturally, I'll start with the fact that we quickly got a cheap and capable model like Opus 5.5 so soon after Fable 5.1, which is actually a side effect of labs like Anthropic having incredibly powerful in-house models than the 230-page Opus 5.5 system card on AI acceleration reveals. And how do the models pass the tests without the laboratories realizing it? And how a leading researcher in another lab inadvertently mocked the idea of ​​a major alignment with a rival lab.  I could go on and on, doubling the length of this video, because we also learned today that there may still be AI agents working to hack into sites like cryptocurrency sites, most likely to make money. These are believed to be "OpenAI" models. Of course, there is also major political news happening at this moment. Lab agreements are being finalized, crazy new AI flaws are being discovered, and much more .  You might now agree with me that even if you spent all your time thinking, reading and using artificial intelligence, you simply couldn't keep up with developments.  Not entirely, at least. Then imagine those who have day-to-day jobs, such as AI researchers and heads of these laboratories.  They may not be keeping up with the news completely.  Now, imagine ordinary people.  As for what this leaves for the press and public oversight of these laboratories, I will leave it up to you to think about. Anyway, here is the official announcement for Opus 5.5. Unlike the GPT-6 Soul, which is clearly inferior to OpenAI's best model, the GPT-6 Astra, I would say that this Opus 5.5 model matches leading capabilities, even by my own benchmark.  Therefore, he truly deserves the attention he receives.  Let me choose just two or three of the metrics that I pay the most attention to.  One of the most difficult scales I have previously covered on this channel is "Terminal Bench Science 0.1". It is a key measure of the models' ability to conduct independent scientific research. On this front, Opus 5.5 lags behind Astra by about 6%, but it is ahead of Fable 5.1. This would indeed be my rough ranking at the moment, as reinforced by the next measure we'll look at, the "Ultimate Test of Humanity, " which measures reasoning across dozens of more complex and obscure domains. Wait, you'll say that the " Opus 5.5" scores much better than the "GPT-6 Astra". According to the scale that was created early last year, every question has a known and unambiguous solution.  Well, it turns out we need a " Humanity's Last Exam Diamond".  It is a version of the scale that has been cleaned up , most likely, to remove incorrect or subjective answers.  In this latest version, "Astra" outperforms "Opus 5.5" by approximately 5%. However, in some forms of long-term programming, "Opus 5.5" may slightly outperform " Astra".  This is according to, for example, the prestigious boundary programming scale.  That ability is, of course, most relevant to artificial intelligence, which develops itself through conducting artificial intelligence research.  Once again, after the news of the past few weeks, it is a gross oversimplification to focus only on the best model at the moment. Ultimately, at the pace we are going, a new model from OpenAI or Anthropic is likely to be released within a week or two .  Advanced AI models, of course, accelerate the development of the next set of advanced models.  As the orange color gets darker in this diagram, you can see the models taking on more and more of the work that goes into creating the next set of AI models. But I mentioned at the beginning that the pace at which prototypes are released and how low their cost is in itself is an indication of the much stronger internal prototypes that these laboratories possess.  I just want to elaborate on that for a moment because that's why we get models like " Opus 5.5" so soon after the release of "5.1".  It is almost certain that Anthropic has a much more capable internal model .  Think of it as "Fable 5.5". His answers to the questions can be distilled into a smaller format such as "Opus 5.5".  Think of a student learning to imitate the teacher's reasoning. Internal models can create problems and tasks for the smaller model, or Learning Reinforcement (RL) environments to train that smaller model. This stronger internal model can be used to evaluate the answer of the smaller model in order to better accelerate its learning process .  None of this is mere speculation, by the way.  I can support each of these points with about twelve research papers.  In more technical terms, a robust internal model can perform what is called core and systems engineering, which is improving how models run on available hardware.    This can make training and inference faster and less expensive for all models in a given laboratory .  You will notice that the Opus 5.5 has seen a decrease in cost. What you may not have noticed is that in the 230- page system card, Anthropic prohibits the use of Opus 5.5 for kernel development.  They don't want other laboratories to use their model to do the same thing.  Is this directed against OpenAI, Meta, or perhaps Chinese labs? videos.transcript_text: Here is GPT-6 at last, and it is indeed a new artificial intelligence model.  But the GPT-6 Astra deserves the new number and name.  And if you know people who haven't followed AI news for weeks or months, their views on models may be more outdated than they realize.  As the title of this video suggests, Astra is a truly impressive model , not just a series of impressive benchmark test results.    It is no marketing ploy to say that Astra's ability to think silently has alarmed many at OpenAI.    The first half of the video will address the reasons why many people, including myself, like him, while the second half will address those concerns.  Of course, this will leave you free to decide what to focus on.  But without further ado, why do people praise him?  Well, one could say the story begins with their main competitor, Anthropic, and the Cloud fable 5.1 model that was released in the last few days . Anthropic could have chosen any metrics to highlight how good Fable 5.1 was, but naturally chose some of the most difficult ones.  I will try to explain how difficult some of these standards are shortly, such as Terminal Bench Science and Automation Bench.  But what you should know is that these are the standards Anthropic has chosen, and they are the same standards in which the GPT-6 Astra outperforms the Fable 5.1 at a lower cost.  We will see this trend in dozens of criteria, but this will only convince those who are truly interested in the best model.  If you believe that all models are overrated and useless , we will have to focus on some of these criteria, starting, for example, with Terminal Bench Science 0.1.  The title is extremely boring, so what does good performance mean in this criterion?  Okay, I'll use the model to explain its performance.  Here is an example of what the model is asked to do using code to answer real scientific questions. The model is given 25,000 brightness readings for three stars, and it should find a slight, recurring decrease in the brightness of these stars.  A program must be written that works on six sets of data that the model cannot see.  The model sees thousands of rows that look similar to these.  Doesn't getting better performance than the experts for just a few dollars now seem impressive ?  What about climate science , with nearly 3 gigabytes of image data?  Thousands of daily photos of 40 lakes in Greenland.  Deduce how and why these lakes dried up, over the course of a season of 153 days, for example.  And remember, these are not just guesses until you get the right result. Models are penalized if they arrive at false hypotheses.  There is also some rather unstructured data , one might say.  Clouds and snow, the model says, can obscure the precise amount of drying on a given day. Therefore, the model needs to link evidence before and after.  I could continue listing examples.  237 MRI images.  Identify, measure, and mark the primary injury in the image.  He analyzed four incorrect answers, all for one standard question. Well, that's just one criterion , but there are many criteria.  What about all the other criteria ?  Let me now turn to the Agent's Last Exam, and yes, I will talk about criteria that OpenAI has not included .  As you may have guessed, in this benchmark, the Astra achieved a new and advanced level of performance, outperforming the Claude Fable 5, and at a much lower cost.  You might quickly say, "Okay, wait a minute, aren't the API prices identical?"  But Astra uses a much smaller number of symbols.  It is more efficient in using codes, and for this reason the cost can be lower.  But this is information for enthusiasts.  I focus more on the skeptics, those who say that these standards do not measure anything real.  Well, the University of California, Berkeley designed the "Agent's Last Exam" to accurately measure real-world things.  Thousands of tasks overseen by experts with verifiable results, across 55 sectors, in tasks of economic value. To illustrate this, here is an example where the model must master industrial manufacturing software.  He needs to use a tool used in real factories and the type of data that humans obtain. Of course, the model does not know what kind of hidden tests its answer will be evaluated on. In this question, as you can see, the evaluator takes a sample of 10,000 points on a hidden reference surface, with the critical points needing to be within a distance of 0.3 mm .  Without knowing this, "Astra" has to plan every piece and avoid collisions, as any collision or cut in the final piece results in a zero.  Or this question is about molten plastic, with the same type of input given to the expert.  Or what about game design where he has to recreate the maps, monsters, and battles of an existing old game with a separate vision model that evaluates every flaw in its output?  I could go on and on .  These standards were designed to be extremely difficult for models to meet. Speaking of vision, let's take a quick look at the ScreenSpot Pro software.    It goes without saying that it has a very high accuracy, reaching about 92%.  I have seen the original research paper, which was published more than a year ago , and you can see the type of software the models are tested on: Adobe Premiere, Photoshop, Office 365 , and many more. Incidentally, the focus here is not on how impressive its output is with these programs, but rather on the model's ability to navigate accurately between these complex screens and interact with highly complex graphical user interfaces.  When we see examples of what Astra can create, which I'm sure you'll try for yourselves, it's because Astra has a superior ability to navigate the computer with very precise interface control, enabling it to produce these impressive results. In other words, these are not imaginary standards, and I have not yet touched upon the most impressive ones.  Let's take a quick look at Level 4 of the Frontier Math test. You will notice for yourselves that it surpasses Fable, albeit at the expense of final performance, but the most important thing is the story of the creation of this benchmark a little over a year ago. This was the most difficult level of math questions, and it was designed by Epoch AI specifically for the Frontier Math test. One mathematics professor at the time said, "I can barely solve some of these problems in my field, so I hope that AI models won't be able to solve any of them correctly. I want them to get zero."  End of quote. At that time, the models received scores close to zero.  For example, Gemini 2.5 Pro.    In fact, GPT 5, which was released almost a year ago, received 10%, 12% and 20%.  Not only did the GPT 6 Astra get a maximum of 98%, but - and we will discuss this later in the video - it got 83% without any explanation.  No need for a notepad , no need for a sequence of thoughts , just give me an answer, 83%. I know there are those who will watch and say, " Okay, but that's just a false standard. What about the real things, the real mathematics?" Okay, let's move on to an assistant professor at Stanford University.  I don't claim to know this result, but he said that GPT-6 significantly surpasses a result reached by, among others, the legendary scientist Terence Tao, and is ten times better in terms of finding the distance between prime numbers.  Not only that, but he created a new and simple starting point for the problem since the 1930s, with this analogy being the basis. This is like discovering a completely new chess opening after decades, going against human tradition.  They won't say it's somewhat similar to move 37. As for the other, more realistic results, what about model development? One OpenAI researcher said, “With Astra, a search integration cycle that used to take me at least a month of full-time work took just over a week, with only a fraction of that time spent actually working on the project . It was literally about immediately improving our next model. I can now feel the power of iterative self-improvement. I also briefly had to revert to using Soul 5.6 internally. That’s when I realized the gap. You don’t always notice an increase in intelligence when you get used to it; you notice it when it’s taken away.” Note, by the way, that free-to-play users won’t get Astra; it will be rolled out to API customers, starting with Pro subscribers and soon to Plus subscribers. But let’s ignore the enthusiasts for a moment and consider what this means for the world. The majority of people don’t use AI at all, and the vast majority of those who do use it use free models. I know it’s a cliché, but the gap between our experience—we who closely follow AI—and the experience of the average person is enormous . No, it seems that we are actually at a critical stage , either all or nothing , or rather a shortened stage. People often say that current models are as bad as they can possibly be , absolutely.
